lead: A regular expression is a pattern written as text that describes a whole set of strings. The re module in Python compares one string against that pattern and reports whether it fits, where it fits and which pieces fit. It exists so that searching, validating and rewriting text does not need a hand-written loop for every case. Common uses are checking a date or PIN, pulling all numbers out of a log line, and replacing phone numbers in a file of customer records. See Unit 3 for plain string methods, which handle simple cases.
prereq: You need: reading lines from a file (5.3) and string methods and slicing (Unit 3).

blocks.text: Most characters in a pattern match themselves. In r'cat', c matches c, a matches a, t matches t. The dot . matches any one character except a newline. A character class in square brackets matches one character from a list or range: [0-9] is any digit, [a-z] any lowercase letter. The shorthand \d means any digit 0-9, \w means a letter, digit or underscore, and \s means a space, tab or newline. The capital forms \D, \W and \S are the negations: \D is any non-digit.

Inside a class, a leading ^ negates: [^0-9] is any non-digit. Outside a class, ^ is an anchor for the start of the string and $ is an anchor for the end. So r'^\d' means the string starts with a digit, and r'\d$' means it ends with one.

Quantifiers repeat the item just before them. \d* is zero or more digits, \d+ is one or more, \d? is zero or one, and \d{4} is exactly four; \d{2,4} allows two, three or four. By default a quantifier is greedy: it takes as many characters as possible. Add ? to make it non-greedy: .+? stops at the first chance.

The vertical bar | means alternation: (cat|dog) matches cat or dog. Parentheses group part of a pattern. Each group is numbered from 1 by its opening parenthesis; group(1), group(2) return the text each group matched. Group 0 is the whole match.

Advanced forms: a named group such as (?P<year>\d{4}) gives a capture group a name — the name must be a valid Python identifier; a backreference \1 reuses the text already captured by group 1; and a lookahead (?=...) checks what follows without consuming it.

sections.h3: The re functions and the match object

blocks.text: re.match(pattern, string) tests only at position 0; it returns a match object or None. re.search(pattern, string) scans forward and returns the first match anywhere, or None. re.findall returns a list of all non-overlapping matches; when the pattern has two or more groups, each list item is a tuple of the group texts, and with one group it is the group text. re.sub(pattern, replacement, string) replaces every match and returns a new string. re.split(pattern, string) cuts the string at each match and returns a list of pieces. re.compile(pattern) builds a pattern object once, for reuse; it has match, search, findall, sub and split methods.

A match object has group(n) for group n, start() for the index where the match begins, end() for the index just after it, and span() for the pair (start, end). Use a raw string for every pattern: r'\d' sends backslash and d to re, while '\d' is an ordinary string in which Python's escape rules apply.

blocks.code:
import re
m = re.match(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', '2024-07-05')
print(m.group(0))
print(m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3))
print(m.start(), m.end())
print(re.findall(r'\d+', 'Anil 78, Bina 91'))
print(re.sub(r'\d+', '#', 'Anil 78, Bina 91'))
print(re.split(r',\s*', 'Anil 78, Bina 91'))

figure.caption: The date is read left to right; positions 0-3 give the year group, positions 5-6 the month and positions 8-9 the day. The dashes at positions 4 and 7 are matched by literal hyphens and belong to no group.

spec.title: Groups in 2024-07-05
spec.aria: The string 2024-07-05 split into single characters, with positions 0 to 3 forming group 1, positions 5 and 6 forming group 2 and positions 8 and 9 forming group 3, and the two dashes left unmarked between the groups.

examples.question: Match the pattern r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})' against the string 2024-07-05 and give every group. Then find all numbers in Anil 78, Bina 91 and replace each number by #.
steps: Import re and call m = re.match(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', '2024-07-05'). The pattern starts with \d{4}, exactly four digits. At position 0 the text is 2024, so group 1 is '2024'.

The next character is '-' at position 4; it is a literal hyphen. Group 2 takes the two digits at positions 5-6: '07'. The hyphen at position 7 is literal. Group 3 takes positions 8-9: '05'. group(0) is the whole match '2024-07-05'. start() is 0 and end() is 10, the length of the string.
re.findall(r'\d+', 'Anil 78, Bina 91') scans all positions. \d+ takes runs of digits: '78' and '91'. The letters, comma and space do not match. Result ['78', '91'].
re.sub(r'\d+', '#', 'Anil 78, Bina 91') replaces each run of digits by #, giving 'Anil #, Bina #'. The replacement string is literal; it is not a pattern.
examples.answer: Group 1 is '2024', group 2 is '07', group 3 is '05', group 0 is '2024-07-05'; findall gives ['78', '91']; sub gives 'Anil #, Bina #'.

import re
m = re.match(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', '2024-07-05')
print(int(m.group(1)))
print(int(m.group(2)))
print(int(m.group(3)))
nums = re.findall(r'\d+', 'Anil 78, Bina 91')
print(int(nums[0]))
print(int(nums[1]))

traps: re.match anchors the pattern at position 0 by itself. A date in the middle of a log line needs re.search, or a leading .* in the pattern.
Write patterns as raw strings. In a normal string '\\d' is backslash and d passed to re, while '\d' relies on an unrecognised escape; r'\d' is clear and correct.
Greedy .* takes the longest possible match, often to the last > or quote. Use .*? when you want the first closing character.
group(0) is the whole match, not the first group. Groups start at 1 in the order of their opening parentheses.
^ inside [ ] negates the class; outside it anchors at the start. [^0-9] is a non-digit, while ^\d means starts with a digit.

quiz.q: What does re.match return when the pattern does not match at position 0?
quiz.a: None. When it matches, it returns a match object.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between \d and \D in a pattern.
quiz.a: \d matches one digit 0-9; \D matches one character that is not a digit.
It returns [('12', '34'), ('56', '78')]. With two groups, findall gives a list of tuples of the two group texts.

quiz.q: For s = (a)(b), compare re.findall(r"\(.*\)", s) and re.findall(r"\(.*?\)", s).
quiz.a: The greedy pattern returns ['(a)(b)']; the non-greedy pattern returns ['(a)', '(b)'].
'a b c'. Each run of whitespace, three spaces then a tab, becomes one space.

quiz.q: A date may appear in the middle of a line. Why can re.match(r'\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}', line) fail while re.search with the same pattern succeeds?
quiz.a: match tests only position 0. If the line has text before the date, no match at position 0. search scans and finds the date later.
A raw string keeps the backslash for re. In an ordinary string, Python's escape rules apply and a backslash may need doubling as '\\d'.

beyond: Not for the exam. Regular expressions are used in log analysis, web form validation, editors, grep and sed, and language lexers. The third-party regex library adds Unicode properties and fuzzy matching. Search for 'Python re HOWTO', 'regex101' and 'catastrophic backtracking' to go deeper. In data work, pandas .str.contains uses the same syntax.
